cases.case_name: Tyner v. Department of Social & Health Services, Child Protective Services
cases.holding: The court held that RCW 26.44.050 impliedly creates a negligent-investigation cause of action in favor of a child's parents, including parents themselves suspected of abuse, and that a later judicial no-contact order does not automatically break legal causation unless all material information was placed before the court.
cases.quote: We conclude that under RCW 26.44.050, CPS owes a duty of care to a child's parents, even those suspected of abusing their own children, when investigating allegations of child abuse.

relevance.INP-01: Establishes that the reporting-and-investigation scheme of chapter 26.44 RCW, which begins with a mandated report, runs to the benefit of parents as well as children.
relevance.INP-04: Holds that the agency's statutory investigative duty exists independently of any court involvement, so a judicially generated referral does not displace the agency's own duty of care.
relevance.DEC-02: Supplies the governing duty standard once a report is accepted: the agency must act reasonably, not flawlessly, toward both child and parents.
relevance.DEC-03: A biased or incomplete investigation that produces a founded finding and separation is actionable against the State.
relevance.DEC-04: Holds that a court order separating parent and child does not cut off State liability where the agency withheld or failed to discover material information.
relevance.ACT-05: Addresses no-contact orders obtained during a CPS investigation and when they do and do not insulate the State from liability.

cases.case_name: M.W. v. Department of Social & Health Services
cases.holding: The court held that the implied negligent-investigation action under RCW 26.44.050 is a narrow exception limited to biased or faulty investigations producing a harmful placement decision, and does not reach other investigative harms such as an intrusive physical examination of the child.
cases.quote: such a claim is available only when DSHS conducts a biased or faulty investigation that leads to a harmful placement decision

relevance.INP-02: Confines the remedy flowing from any report, mandated or citizen, to harms caused by a resulting placement decision.
relevance.INP-07: The claimed harm arose from investigators' physical examination of the child, and the court held that such investigative harm is outside the statutory cause of action.
relevance.INP-10: Marks the outer boundary of agency exposure once an intake is escalated to a full investigation.
relevance.DEC-01: Because only harmful placement decisions are actionable, a screen-out or unfounded closure standing alone will rarely support the statutory claim.
relevance.DEC-02: Defines the narrow-exception framework governing the quality of an accepted investigation.
relevance.ACT-03: Identifies placing a child in an abusive home, removing a child from a nonabusive home, or failing to remove as the three actionable placement harms.
relevance.ACT-06: Holds that an intrusive investigative medical examination of the child is not itself a compensable harm under RCW 26.44.050.

cases.case_name: Ducote v. Department of Social & Health Services
cases.holding: The court held that stepparents are not within the class protected by RCW 26.44.050 and therefore lack standing to bring a negligent-investigation claim, limiting the protected class to children, parents, guardians and custodians.
cases.quote: they are not included in the categories of persons who may sue for negligent investigation under RCW 26.44.050

relevance.DEC-01: Defines who may challenge an agency investigative decision at all, which determines who can litigate a screening or unfounded determination.
relevance.DEC-03: A stepparent stigmatized by a founded finding has no statutory negligent-investigation remedy, however damaging the finding.
relevance.ACT-05: Ducote was barred from his home and from contact with his stepchildren, yet the court held he was outside the statute's protected class.

cases.holding: The court held that the statutory duty to investigate is triggered only by a report of abuse or neglect that has already occurred, so a parent's prediction of future harm from a proposed placement did not invoke DSHS's duty under former RCW 26.44.050.
cases.quote: Generally, a report initiates the dependency process. The duty to investigate cannot be invoked until receipt of a report.

relevance.INP-01: Defines what a mandated reporter must communicate before the agency's investigative duty attaches: past or ongoing conduct, not a prediction.
relevance.INP-02: A parent's warning about future danger was held not to be a duty-triggering report under chapter 26.44 RCW.
relevance.INP-06: Fixes the threshold content a hotline communication must have to qualify as a report that starts the investigative clock.
relevance.INP-08: Supplies the case-by-case test for whether any informant's communication, including a school report, constitutes a duty-triggering report.
relevance.INP-10: Where no qualifying report exists there is nothing to escalate, and the court will not assess the sufficiency of any investigation performed.
relevance.DEC-01: Directly governs screen-out liability: without a qualifying report there is no investigative duty and no negligent-investigation claim.
relevance.DEC-02: Explains which communications the agency must accept for investigation and which it may decline.
relevance.ACT-04: The child was placed with a relative over the mother's objection and later died; the court held the placement inquiry fell outside RCW 26.44.050.
relevance.OUT-06: Arises from a child fatality in an agency-approved placement and defines the limits of the State's statutory tort exposure.
relevance.FAIL-04: Shows that a death following an agency placement decision does not by itself establish a breach of the statutory investigative duty.

cases.holding: The court held that caseworkers and DSHS have only qualified, not absolute, immunity for reporting and investigating child abuse and for placing names on the central registry, and that the good-faith condition of the RCW 26.44.060 immunity is a question of fact.
cases.quote: The determination of good faith under RCW 26.44.060 necessarily presents issues of fact.

relevance.INP-01: Defines the scope of the reporter immunity mandated reporters rely on: it is qualified and conditioned on good faith.
relevance.INP-02: Confirms that the RCW 26.44.060 immunity protecting voluntary reporters is qualified and turns on objective reasonableness.
relevance.INP-06: Good-faith immunity for hotline reporting is not absolute and cannot be resolved as a matter of law on disputed facts.
relevance.INP-08: The plaintiffs were ranch employees accused of failing to report, which frames the exposure of professional reporters on both sides of the duty.
relevance.DEC-03: Holds that listing a person on the central registry after a founded determination is not protected by absolute immunity.

cases.case_name: Miles v. Child Protective Services Department
cases.holding: The court affirmed dismissal of claims arising from an emergency removal, holding the caseworker was entitled to the good-faith immunity of RCW 26.44.056(3) where she relied on the opinions of treating physicians, and that the parents identified no clearly established constitutional right to support their section 1983 claim.
cases.quote: We conclude that a rational trier could not find causation, and that a rational trier would be obligated to find good faith.

relevance.INP-03: Illustrates the joint hospital, law-enforcement and CPS pathway into protective custody and the immunity that attaches to it.
relevance.INP-07: The removal rested on the diagnoses of hospital physicians, and reliance on those medical opinions supported the caseworker's good faith.
relevance.INP-12: Applies RCW 26.44.056(3) good-faith immunity to the decision to take a child into protective custody.
relevance.DEC-04: Supplies the state-law immunity standard governing the emergency removal decision itself.
relevance.FAIL-02: Shows what a section 1983 wrongful-removal plaintiff must identify, a clearly established right, and why the claim failed here.

cases.holding: In a foster-care class action the court recognized that foster children hold a substantive due process right to be free from unreasonable risk of harm and to reasonable safety, but held the jury was misinstructed by treating the professional-judgment standard of care as the right itself, and it narrowed the systemwide injunction.
cases.quote: We hold that foster children have a constitutional substantive due process right to be free from unreasonable risks of harm and a right to reasonable safety.

relevance.INP-09: The leading Washington example of systemic litigation producing court-supervised reform of the child welfare agency.
relevance.ACT-03: Establishes the constitutional floor the State owes every child it places in foster care.
relevance.OUT-04: The class included youth who had aged out of care, and the court addressed their continuing stake in the systemic remedy.
relevance.OUT-06: Frames serious harm in care as a constitutional violation rather than merely a services failure.
relevance.FAIL-03: The court dismissed most federal child welfare statutory claims, showing the limits of privately enforcing federal compliance standards.
relevance.FAIL-04: Supplies the deliberate-indifference culpability floor for measuring State responsibility for harm to a child in its custody.
relevance.PMC-01: Judicially imposed outcome measures in this case parallel the federal CFSR safety and permanency benchmarks.
relevance.PMC-02: The court limited evidence of fiscal constraints, framing how funding is treated when agency performance is audited in court.
relevance.PMC-03: Demonstrates the role of independent external review, the function CAPTA assigns to citizen review panels.
relevance.PMC-04: Establishes the constitutional standard against which fatality and serious-harm reviews of children in care are measured.
relevance.PMC-06: Provides judicially recognized systemwide performance benchmarks against which aggregate analysis of agency practice can be tested.

cases.holding: The court held that DSHS stands in a Restatement section 315(b) protective special relationship with dependent foster children based on entrustment and vulnerability rather than physical custody, and that the children's negligence claims for failure to protect them from their foster parents must go to a jury.
cases.quote: Consistent with our precedent, we hold that the special relationship between DSHS and foster children gives rise to a protective duty under Restatement § 315(b).

relevance.INP-09: Holds the agency answerable in tort for failing to perform required health and safety checks, the very practice oversight bodies audit.
relevance.ACT-03: Establishes the common law duty of reasonable care the agency owes each child it places in foster care.
relevance.OUT-06: Recognizes a damages remedy for serious harm suffered by a child while in agency-supervised placement.
relevance.FAIL-04: Failure to conduct required health and safety visits over a full year was held sufficient evidence of breach for a jury.
relevance.PMC-01: Ties the agency's monitoring obligations, visits, safety checks and placement oversight, to an enforceable legal duty.
relevance.PMC-04: Supplies the negligence framework under which serious harm to a supervised child is reviewed after the fact.

cases.holding: The court held that the discretionary right to counsel for children in RCW 13.34.100(7)(a) satisfies article I, section 3, and further held that the confidentiality of juvenile dependency records under RCW 13.50.100(2) survives appeal so appellate courts should seal such records on their own motion.
cases.quote: we hold that the confidential nature of dependency proceedings granted by RCW 13.50.100(2) is not lost through appeal

relevance.OUT-04: Governs appointment of counsel for older dependent youth whose own interests in placement and transition planning may diverge from the agency's.
relevance.FAIL-06: Defines the confidentiality baseline, so an unauthorized release of dependency records, not a refusal to release, is the disclosure failure here.
relevance.PMC-03: Sets the statutory confidentiality limits any external review body must work within when examining dependency case files.
relevance.PMC-05: Holds that chapter 13.50 RCW confidentiality is not waived by appeal, a direct constraint on public access to dependency records.

cases.holding: The court held that children in dependency and termination proceedings have liberty interests at least as weighty as their parents' and may constitutionally be entitled to appointed counsel, but that RCW 13.34.100(6) is constitutionally adequate because the right is not universal and is committed case by case to the trial judge's discretion.
cases.quote: We hold the due process right of children who are subjects of dependency or termination proceedings to counsel is not universal.

relevance.OUT-04: Recognizes the child's own liberty interest in placement and family relationships, which matters most as a youth approaches majority.
relevance.FAIL-03: Holds that appellate review, rather than a categorical rule, is the mechanism for protecting a child's counsel right.
relevance.PMC-01: Articulates the child-centered interests, safety, family integrity and stability, that federal performance review also measures.

cases.case_name: In re Parental Rights to K.M.M.
cases.holding: The court held that current parental unfitness must be assessed in relation to the particular child, so that remedying general parental deficiencies is not dispositive and a parent who cannot meet a specific child's basic needs may be found currently unfit.
cases.quote: in order to determine whether a parent is a fit parent to a particular child, the court must determine that the parent is able to meet that child's basic needs

relevance.OUT-01: Explains why correcting identified deficiencies does not automatically compel return of the child.
relevance.OUT-02: Supplies the governing test for the constitutionally required finding of current parental unfitness.
relevance.FAIL-01: Sets the standard an appellate court applies when reviewing whether an unfitness finding was properly made.

cases.case_name: In re Parental Rights to K.J.B.
cases.holding: The court held that RCW 13.34.180(1)(f) makes consideration of the incarcerated-parent factors mandatory even though express written findings on them are not required, and reversed a termination where the trial court failed to consider them.
cases.quote: We hold that while explicit findings on the incarcerated parent factors are not statutorily required, consideration of the factors is mandatory.

relevance.OUT-02: Governs how an incarcerated parent's circumstances must be weighed before parental rights may be terminated.
relevance.FAIL-01: A termination order was reversed and remanded solely because the court omitted a mandatory statutory consideration.

cases.case_name: In re Parental Rights to B.P.
cases.holding: The court reversed a termination, holding that where a child's special needs are exacerbated by the State's failure to timely provide the biological parent with the same necessary services it gave the foster parents, the State has not proved the RCW 13.34.180(1)(d) prerequisite absent a showing of futility.
cases.quote: The trial court may not terminate a parent's rights unless it determines that the Department fulfilled that duty or that services would be futile.

relevance.ACT-01: Defines the content of the services the agency must actually deliver to the parent, not merely offer on paper.
relevance.ACT-02: Holds that court-ordered service plans must include the services the parent needs to meet the child's identified special needs.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification cannot be foreclosed by a services gap the agency itself created.
relevance.OUT-02: States the statutory services prerequisite and the narrow futility exception that must be satisfied before termination.
relevance.FAIL-01: The Supreme Court reversed both the Court of Appeals and the termination order for failure of proof on a statutory element.

cases.holding: The court reversed a termination and dismissed the proceeding, holding that where the State provided the foster parent but not the mother with training needed to manage the child's ADHD, it failed to prove that all necessary services capable of correcting the parental deficiency had been offered.
cases.quote: Since this training, deemed necessary to address C.S.'s behavioral problems, was not offered to Ms. Sampey, termination of her parental rights was not warranted

relevance.ACT-01: Confirms that the services obligation extends to any condition preventing reunification, however the agency labels it.
relevance.ACT-02: Holds the agency cannot withhold from the parent a service it supplies to the foster caregiver and then rely on the resulting gap.
relevance.DEC-06: Reinforces that the statutory scheme is directed at correcting conditions and reuniting families rather than escalating to termination.
relevance.OUT-01: The mother had corrected her identified deficiency, and the court held the case should have moved toward reunification.
relevance.OUT-05: The court did not merely reverse but dismissed the termination proceeding outright.

cases.holding: The court adopted a broad reading of the ICWA and WICWA inquiry threshold, holding that a court has reason to know a child is an Indian child whenever any participant in the proceeding indicates the child has tribal heritage, and that the trial court had reason to know at the shelter care hearing.
cases.quote: We hold that a trial court has "reason to know" that a child is an Indian child when a participant in the proceeding indicates that the child has tribal heritage.

relevance.INP-11: Sets the trigger for ICWA and WICWA jurisdiction and notice in Washington dependency cases.
relevance.DEC-05: Requires the inquiry into Indian status at the earliest hearing, so ICWA protections attach when the petition is filed.
relevance.FAIL-03: Failure to apply the correct reason-to-know standard is itself a compliance failure requiring reversal.
relevance.FAIL-05: Adopts a broad standard precisely to respect tribal sovereignty and to counteract the historical removal of Native children.

cases.holding: The court held that the Department failed to make active efforts under ICWA and WICWA where the social worker offered a case plan and one phone call but did not actively help the parent access services, and that declining voluntary services before a dependency finding cannot substitute for active efforts.
cases.quote: We hold that the Department in the present case did not engage in active efforts as is required under ICWA and WICWA.

relevance.INP-05: Holds that a parent's refusal of voluntary pre-dependency services cannot later be used against her as proof of agency effort.
relevance.INP-11: Applies the heightened ICWA and WICWA active-efforts duty owed before an Indian child may be removed.
relevance.ACT-01: Distinguishes voluntary services from the affirmative, hands-on assistance ICWA requires.
relevance.DEC-06: Clarifies the legal consequence of a family declining an alternative-response style voluntary service offer.

cases.holding: The court held that ICWA and WICWA protect the parental rights of a non-Indian parent of an Indian child, apply to stepparent adoptions, require any party seeking termination including a private petitioner to prove active efforts, and that WICWA legislatively abrogated the existing Indian family exception.
cases.quote: We hold that the plain language of ICWA and WICWA apply to and protect the parental rights of a non-Indian parent of an Indian child.

relevance.INP-11: Defines the reach of ICWA and WICWA by the child's status, not the parent's, in every child custody proceeding.
relevance.OUT-02: Requires active efforts proof from any party seeking termination, including in a private stepparent adoption.
relevance.FAIL-05: Holds the existing Indian family exception, long criticized as a vehicle for bypassing tribal protections, abrogated in Washington.

cases.holding: The court held that the ICWA active-efforts showing under 25 U.S.C. section 1912(d) need be proved only by clear, cogent and convincing evidence rather than beyond a reasonable doubt, and that a parent's voluntary unavailability excuses the State from offering further remedial services.
cases.quote: We conclude that the trial court properly applied the clear, cogent and convincing standard to the requirements contained in 25 U.S.C. § 1912(d).

relevance.INP-11: Fixes the evidentiary standard governing the federal active-efforts element in Washington ICWA cases.
relevance.ACT-02: Holds a parent's unwillingness or inability to use offered services excuses the agency from providing more.
relevance.FAIL-03: Identifies which ICWA findings carry the beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard and which do not, a frequent source of compliance error.

cases.holding: The court held that a parent's assertion of Cherokee heritage gave the trial court reason to know an Indian child might be involved and triggered the ICWA and state notice duties, that the burden of ensuring notice rests on the court and the State rather than the parent, and that remand for proper notice is the ordinary remedy.
cases.quote: Dunlavy's assertion of Cherokee heritage gave the court "reason to know," and triggered the notice requirements of 25 U.S.C. § 1912(a) and RCW 13.34.070(10).

relevance.INP-11: Holds that tribal enrollment is not required to trigger ICWA notice and that only the tribe can decide membership.
relevance.DEC-05: Places the notice burden on the court and the petitioning agency from the moment the proceeding is opened.

cases.holding: The court held that establishing a guardianship under chapter 13.36 RCW by a preponderance of the evidence satisfies due process, because parents retain visitation and modification rights and a guardianship does not sever the parent-child relationship as termination does.
cases.quote: Since guardianships under the new statute do not rise to the level of terminations, proceedings to establish guardianships do not warrant the same standard of proof as termination proceedings.

relevance.OUT-03: Supplies the constitutional standard of proof and the due process analysis governing dependency guardianships in Washington.

cases.holding: The court vacated a dependency guardianship and remanded for reinstatement of the dependency, holding that a guardianship may not be imposed where the father had remedied his parental deficiencies so the child could be returned to his care in the near future.
cases.quote: We conclude that because the father has remedied his parental deficiencies, D.S. can be returned to his father's care in the near future.

relevance.OUT-01: Holds that reunification, not guardianship, is required once the parent has corrected the conditions that caused removal.
relevance.OUT-03: Defines the statutory limits on when a guardianship may substitute for reunification or termination.
relevance.OUT-05: Orders the guardianship vacated and the dependency reinstated rather than the case closed to permanency.

cases.holding: The court held that a juvenile court's practice of sealing parents' ex parte motions for public funding of expert services violated GR 15 and article I, section 10 because no Ishikawa analysis was performed, and that applying GR 15's notice requirements in termination cases comports with due process.
cases.quote: We hold that the superior court's ex parte sealing practice and the sealing of the disputed documents violate the court rules and Washington Constitution article I, section 10.

relevance.INP-09: Establishes that the open-courts guarantee constrains how juvenile courts shield their own dependency records from review.
relevance.FAIL-06: Blanket, unanalyzed sealing of dependency court records is itself a transparency violation under article I, section 10.
relevance.PMC-03: Defines the balance between parental privacy and public scrutiny that any external review of dependency practice must observe.
relevance.PMC-05: Requires a case-specific Ishikawa showing before dependency court records may be withheld from the public.
relevance.PMC-06: Supplies the constitutional presumption of openness that makes systematic review of dependency court records possible.

cases.case_name: Wright v. Department of Social & Health Services
cases.holding: The court held that the Public Records Act does not reach juvenile records governed by chapter 13.50 RCW, which supplies the exclusive route to such records through a motion in juvenile court, and reversed the PRA penalties awarded against DSHS.
cases.quote: We hold that the PRA does not apply to chapter 13.50 RCW juvenile records

relevance.FAIL-06: Holds that non-production of juvenile records in response to a PRA request is not a PRA violation, which shapes what counts as a disclosure failure.
relevance.PMC-05: Identifies chapter 13.50 RCW, not the PRA, as the exclusive mechanism for obtaining Washington child welfare juvenile records.
relevance.PMC-06: Defines the statutory channel that any systematic records-based analysis of Washington child welfare data must use.

cases.case_name: Hardee v. Department of Social & Health Services
cases.holding: The court held that due process is satisfied by the preponderance of the evidence standard in an administrative proceeding revoking a home child care license, and that the review judge's findings were supported by substantial evidence.
cases.quote: Due process is satisfied by application of the preponderance of the evidence standard to the revocation of a home child care license, as provided by RCW 43.215.300(2).

relevance.DEC-03: Supplies the evidentiary standard and due process analysis governing administrative adjudication of child-safety findings against an individual.
relevance.FAIL-01: Frames the scope of judicial review of an agency adjudication under the Administrative Procedure Act, including issue-preservation limits.
relevance.PMC-02: Shows how agency licensing and compliance determinations are tested on administrative review.

cases.holding: The court affirmed a termination, holding that DSHS proved every RCW 13.34.180(1) element by clear, cogent and convincing evidence and that the parent failed to establish ineffective assistance of counsel under the Strickland deficiency-and-prejudice test.
cases.quote: To establish ineffective assistance of counsel, a party must show deficient performance and resulting prejudice.

relevance.ACT-05: The mother's refusal to recognize the danger posed by continued contact with the father drove both the service plan and the termination.
relevance.FAIL-01: States the two-part standard a parent must satisfy to obtain reversal of a termination for ineffective assistance of counsel.

cases.holding: The court reversed a termination, holding the parent had not forfeited his right to counsel by delay or nonappearance and that denying newly appointed counsel a continuance to prepare deprived him of effective assistance and was an abuse of discretion.
cases.quote: the trial court's decision to deny the motion to continue the termination trial deprived Ramsey of the right to effective assistance of counsel and was an abuse of discretion

relevance.FAIL-01: A termination order was reversed for a procedural denial of the parent's right to effective counsel, without reaching the evidence.

cases.holding: The court held that a parent has a substantive due process right to pursue voluntary relinquishment as an alternative to involuntary termination, and vacated the termination so the juvenile court could first determine the disabled father's competence to relinquish.
cases.quote: We hold that a parent has a substantive due process right to pursue voluntary relinquishment of his or her parental rights as an alternative to involuntary termination.

relevance.INP-05: Recognizes a parent-initiated route out of the case that the court must consider before imposing an involuntary outcome.
relevance.FAIL-05: The father's cognitive disability required a competency determination before his rights could be involuntarily terminated.

cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of the rights of two parents with chronic mental illness, holding that the ADA requires reasonable accommodation but not services unavailable to others, that the failure of a single referral does not defeat the services element, and that the issue at termination is current unfitness rather than the original dependency grounds.
cases.quote: The Act does not require public entities to provide the disabled with services not offered to others.

relevance.ACT-02: Holds that one unsuccessful service referral does not preclude a finding that all necessary available services were offered.
relevance.FAIL-05: States the ADA reasonable-accommodation standard and its limits in Washington termination proceedings.

cases.holding: The court held that while sibling-relationship evidence is not categorically irrelevant at termination, RCW 13.34.200(3) requires only a statement in the termination order about sibling relationships and does not make their status an element, so excluding further sibling evidence was not an abuse of discretion.
cases.quote: the status of sibling relations is not a required element to support a termination finding

relevance.ACT-04: Catalogs the statutory provisions favoring sibling placement, visitation and contact throughout the dependency scheme.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment requires a State to support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before it may permanently sever the rights of parents in their natural child.
cases.quote: at a parental rights termination proceeding, a near-equal allocation of risk between the parents and the State is constitutionally intolerable

relevance.OUT-02: Supplies the federal constitutional floor, at least clear and convincing evidence, for every termination of parental rights.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: Sitting en banc in a case arising from the Wenatchee, Washington child sex abuse investigations, the court held there is no constitutional right to have child witnesses interviewed in a particular manner, and that a deliberate-fabrication claim requires evidence that investigators knew or should have known the accused was innocent or used techniques so coercive they knew would yield false information.
cases.quote: an allegation that an interviewer disbelieved an initial denial and continued with aggressive questioning of the child cannot, without more, support a deliberate-fabrication-of-evidence claim

relevance.INP-03: Arose from a joint police and CPS investigation in Washington and defines the constitutional limits on that joint interviewing practice.
relevance.INP-08: Holds there is no federal constitutional right to a particular child-interview protocol, however flawed the questioning.
relevance.DEC-02: Sets the constitutional floor, and the wide latitude, governing how investigators may question child witnesses.
relevance.FAIL-02: Supplies the Ninth Circuit's controlling two-branch test for a section 1983 deliberate-fabrication claim against child abuse investigators.

cases.case_name: Costanich v. Department of Social & Health Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: In a case against Washington DSHS the court held that deliberately fabricating evidence in civil child abuse proceedings violates Fourteenth Amendment due process where a liberty or property interest is at stake, but granted qualified immunity because that right was not clearly established when the 2001 investigation occurred.
cases.quote: We conclude that deliberately fabricating evidence in civil child abuse proceedings violates the Due Process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment when a liberty or property interest is at stake

relevance.DEC-03: Holds that a caseworker who deliberately falsifies the record supporting a founded finding violates due process.
relevance.DEC-05: The fabricated declaration supported a guardianship termination petition, the point at which the case moved into court.
relevance.FAIL-02: Extends the Devereaux fabrication rule from criminal to civil child welfare proceedings against Washington officials.
relevance.PMC-02: Frames the accountability consequences when an agency investigation is shown to rest on falsified evidence.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held the complaint plausibly alleged Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment violations where a caseworker removed a child without a court order despite having no reasonable cause to believe she was in imminent danger and having time to seek a warrant, but affirmed dismissal of the judicial deception claim.
cases.quote: Such "reasonable cause" arises, for example, where there is evidence of imminent abuse after sufficient investigation.

relevance.INP-03: Describes the investigation an official must complete before an emergency referral can ripen into lawful warrantless custody.
relevance.INP-06: Holds that an uncorroborated report does not supply reasonable cause when further investigation was feasible.
relevance.INP-12: States the reasonable-cause-plus-imminence standard governing warrantless protective custody in the Ninth Circuit.
relevance.DEC-04: Holds the scope and duration of the intrusion must remain justified by the exigency that allowed the removal.
relevance.ACT-06: The child was transferred to a behavioral health facility on a temporary custody notice, and continued detention after clinicians found her low risk was held actionable.
relevance.FAIL-02: Supplies the elements of a Ninth Circuit section 1983 claim for removal without exigency and for judicial deception.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: Sitting en banc the court reaffirmed that officials must ordinarily obtain prior judicial authorization before removing a child, warrantless seizure being excusable only on reasonable cause to believe the child is likely to suffer serious bodily harm in the time needed to get a warrant, and held the facts there met that standard.
cases.quote: Under the Fourth Amendment, government officials are ordinarily required to obtain prior judicial authorization before removing a child from the custody of her parent.

relevance.INP-12: States the controlling Fourth Amendment rule for protective custody in the circuit that governs Washington.
relevance.ACT-03: Establishes that a court order is the default prerequisite to any placement of a child outside the home.
relevance.DEC-04: Supplies the exigency test the emergency removal decision must satisfy to avoid constitutional liability.
relevance.FAIL-02: Defines when a removal without prior judicial authorization becomes an unconstitutional seizure.

cases.case_name: Mann v. County of San Diego
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that subjecting children in protective custody to invasive investigatory medical examinations without notifying the parents and without parental consent or judicial authorization violates the parents' Fourteenth Amendment right to family association and the children's Fourth Amendment rights, absent exigency.
cases.quote: the County violated the Mann children's Fourth Amendment rights by failing to obtain a warrant or to provide these constitutional safeguards before subjecting the children to these invasive medical examinations

relevance.INP-07: Holds that an investigatory medical examination of a child requires parental notice and consent or a court order.
relevance.INP-12: Limits what the State may do to a child after taking protective custody, not merely how it may take custody.
relevance.ACT-06: Directly governs authorization for medical or forensic examination of a child in agency custody.
relevance.FAIL-02: Establishes municipal liability where a county's routine practice of examining children without parental notice violates the Constitution.

cases.holding: The court held that the implied negligent-investigation action under chapter 26.44 RCW reaches only an investigation that leads to a harmful placement decision by the State, and refused to extend it to a 'constructive placement' where the parents themselves sent the child out of the home, affirming dismissal of a jury award arising from the Wenatchee investigations.
cases.quote: We decline Petitioners' request to enlarge the negligent investigation cause of action under chapter 26.44 RCW to include speculative harms argued as "constructive placement."

relevance.DEC-01: Holds that an investigation producing no agency placement decision, however negligent, supports no statutory claim, which is the posture after a screen-out or unfounded closure.
relevance.DEC-02: Confirms that the quality of an accepted investigation is actionable only through the placement decision it produces, not through the investigation's other consequences.
relevance.ACT-03: Rejects constructive placement, the family's own decision to send the child away, as a substitute for the State placement decision the cause of action requires.

cases.holding: The court held that DSHS caseworkers have no absolute immunity for foster placement decisions made outside an adversarial judicial process, that they may claim only the Guffey qualified immunity, which requires carrying out a statutory duty by statutory procedures and acting reasonably, and that the State itself has no immunity from suit.
cases.quote: Caseworkers cannot claim even a qualified immunity when they fail to follow statutory procedures.

relevance.INP-04: Holds that a court order procured ex parte and without any adversarial evaluation of the placement does not confer absolute immunity on the caseworkers who obtained it.
relevance.DEC-04: Limits caseworker immunity for removal and placement to a qualified immunity that fails whenever the statutory procedures were not followed.
relevance.ACT-03: The foundational Washington authority on what immunity, if any, attaches to a foster care placement decision and the investigation preceding it.

cases.case_name: Yonker v. Department of Social & Health Services
cases.holding: The court held that the public duty doctrine does not shield DSHS from a negligence claim by a mother and child whose reports of possible abuse the Department declined to investigate, because they fall within the particular and circumscribed class chapter 26.44 RCW was enacted to protect, and reversed summary judgment for the State.
cases.quote: If there is a question whether a report is sufficient to invoke the duty to investigate, that issue will be resolved on a case-by-case basis.

relevance.INP-01: The origin of the enforceable investigative duty under chapter 26.44 RCW, on facts where caseworkers agreed the report indicated possible abuse and still did nothing.
relevance.INP-02: Holds that a non-mandated parent-reporter and her child are within the particular and circumscribed class the Legislature intended chapter 26.44 RCW to protect.
relevance.INP-06: Announces the case-by-case test for whether an intake communication is sufficient to invoke the Department's duty to investigate.
relevance.INP-08: Supplies the case-by-case sufficiency test that governs any informant's report, the rule Wrigley later adopts verbatim.
relevance.DEC-01: Holds DSHS may be sued for declining to investigate a report its own caseworkers acknowledged could indicate abuse.
relevance.DEC-02: Establishes that the duty to accept and investigate is judicially enforceable and is not defeated by the public duty doctrine.

cases.holding: The court held that an order permanently depriving a parent of the custody of his children must rest on clear, cogent and convincing evidence, meaning the ultimate fact in issue must be shown to be highly probable, and on that standard sustained the deprivation order the Court of Appeals had reversed.
cases.quote: clear, cogent and convincing evidence is necessary to sustain an order permanently depriving a parent of the care, custody and control of his children

relevance.OUT-02: The foundational Washington statement of the standard of proof for permanent deprivation and of what clear, cogent and convincing means in practice.
relevance.FAIL-01: Defines the appellate standard, substantial evidence measured against the highly probable test, by which a termination is reviewed for sufficiency.

cases.holding: The court held that before restricting public access to a hearing or its records a trial court must follow five steps, a specific showing of need, an opportunity for those present to object, consideration of the least restrictive effective means, a weighing of competing interests stated in specific findings, and an order no broader in application or duration than necessary; it found the closure erroneous and remanded the continued sealing for reconsideration.
cases.quote: Each time restrictions on access to criminal hearings or the records from hearings are sought, courts must follow these steps

relevance.FAIL-06: Supplies the five-step test whose omission is what makes a court's sealing of dependency records a transparency violation.
relevance.PMC-05: The controlling Washington framework a court must apply before any court record, including a dependency file, may be withheld from the public.
relevance.PMC-06: Establishes the presumption of openness and places the burden on the party seeking secrecy, which is what makes systematic review of court records possible.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause does not require appointment of counsel for an indigent parent in every parental termination proceeding, and left the question to the trial court in the first instance under the Mathews v. Eldridge factors, subject to appellate review.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

relevance.OUT-04: The federal baseline for appointed counsel on which Washington's discretionary, case-by-case rule for dependent children and older youth is built.
relevance.FAIL-01: Holds that the counsel question is committed to the trial court in the first instance subject to appellate review, which is the corrective mechanism when counsel is wrongly denied.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: A four-Justice plurality held that Washington's nonparental visitation statute, as applied to order grandparent visitation over the objection of a fit custodial mother without according her decision any material weight, unconstitutionally infringed her Fourteenth Amendment right to make decisions concerning the care, custody and control of her children.
cases.quote: there is a presumption that fit parents act in the best interests of their children

relevance.ACT-04: Holds that a fit parent's decision about a relative's contact with her children carries a presumption of validity a court may not simply override.
relevance.OUT-03: Sets the constitutional limit on transferring custody or visitation rights to relatives over the objection of a fit parent.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that officials may not remove children without prior judicial authorization absent reasonable cause to believe the child is in imminent danger of serious bodily injury with the intrusion no broader than necessary to avert it, and that, barring a reasonable concern that physical evidence will dissipate or an urgent medical problem, the State must notify parents and obtain judicial approval before subjecting a seized child to an investigatory physical examination.
cases.quote: the state is required to notify parents and to obtain judicial approval before children are subjected to investigatory physical examinations

relevance.INP-07: The root Ninth Circuit authority requiring parental notice and judicial approval before an investigatory physical examination of a child.
relevance.INP-12: States the reasonable-cause-plus-imminence rule and the scope limitation governing warrantless protective custody in the circuit that governs Washington.
relevance.ACT-06: Directly governs whether officials may subject a child already in protective custody to an invasive medical or forensic examination.
relevance.FAIL-02: The foundational section 1983 authority on unlawful removal and on municipal liability for a custom of seizing and examining children without constitutional safeguards.

cases.case_name: Rogers v. County of San Joaquin
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that warrantless removal of children is permissible only in cases of exigency, meaning reasonable cause to believe the child is likely to experience serious bodily harm in the time required to obtain a warrant, and reversed qualified immunity for the social worker because no reasonable social worker could have believed an exigency existed on this record.
cases.quote: we hold that it was clearly established that warrantless removal of children is permissible only in cases of exigency

relevance.INP-03: Applies the same exigency requirement to social workers and to the police officer who accompanied the removal, so a referral between them does not lower the constitutional threshold.
relevance.INP-12: The source of the 'likely to experience serious bodily harm in the time that would be required to obtain a warrant' formulation that Keates quotes and Kirkpatrick applies.
relevance.DEC-04: States the exigency test the emergency removal decision must satisfy and holds that no reasonable social worker could have found exigency here.
relevance.FAIL-02: Denies qualified immunity for a warrantless removal, showing when an unlawful-removal claim survives past the immunity stage.

cases.case_name: Deer v. Department of Social & Health Services
cases.holding: The court affirmed dismissal of a public disclosure act suit for dependency records, holding that chapter 13.50 RCW is an 'other statute' exemption that supplements the act and supplies the exclusive process, a motion in juvenile court, for obtaining juvenile justice and care records.
cases.quote: chapter 13.50 RCW supplements the PDA and provides the exclusive process for obtaining juvenile justice and care records

relevance.FAIL-06: Holds that refusing a public records request for dependency records is not a disclosure violation, because those records lie outside the act entirely.
relevance.PMC-05: The original holding, later followed in Wright, that chapter 13.50 RCW rather than the public records act is the exclusive route to Washington juvenile dependency records.
relevance.PMC-06: Identifies the juvenile court motion process that any systematic records-based analysis of Washington child welfare case data must use.

cases.holding: The court affirmed a termination, holding that the clear, cogent and convincing weight of the evidence showed all necessary, reasonably available services capable of correcting the parental deficiencies had been offered, and that a parent's own unwillingness or inability to use the services provided excuses the State from offering more.
cases.quote: a parent's unwillingness or inability to make use of the services provided excuses the State from offering extra services that might have been helpful

relevance.ACT-01: The source of the rule that a parent's unwillingness or inability to use the services provided excuses the State from offering more, whether those services are voluntary or ordered.
relevance.ACT-02: Holds that unanimous expert proof that the parent's deficiencies were untreatable satisfied the statutory requirement that all necessary services had been offered.

cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for DSHS, holding that a dependency court's order is a superseding intervening cause cutting off caseworker liability for negligent investigation unless the faulty investigation deprived that court of material information, and that Petcu identified no material information withheld from the dependency judge.
cases.quote: Otherwise, court intervention operates as a superseding intervening cause that cuts off the caseworker's liability.

relevance.INP-04: Defines when judicial involvement in a case breaks the causal chain between the agency's own investigation and the resulting separation of parent and child.
relevance.DEC-05: Holds that once the dependency petition is before a court, the court's findings cut off agency liability unless the supporting investigation concealed material facts.

notes: Every case listed was retrieved from CourtListener in this session and its opinion text read. Each quote was machine-verified as an exact substring of the majority or lead opinion (whitespace and curly quotation marks normalized). No unpublished memorandum decisions were used, and no dissent, concurrence, syllabus or headnote was quoted; for M.W. v. DSHS and In re Parental Rights to K.J.B. the lead/majority opinion id was used deliberately because CourtListener's default hit returned the dissent.

Washington's intermediate court (court_id washctapp) is a single Court of Appeals sitting in three divisions; the division appears in the reporter only, so no court designator is added to Wn. App. citations.

Where the CourtListener cluster carried only a regional-reporter citation (H.B.H. v. State, In re Dependency of Schermer, In re Dependency of E.H., In re Dependency of J.D.P.), the citation is given in P.3d form with a court designator rather than asserting an unverified Wn.2d or Wn. App. 2d page number. Lawyers should add the official parallel cite (H.B.H. is 192 Wn.2d 154; Schermer is 161 Wn.2d 927; E.H. is 191 Wn.2d 872) after independent confirmation.

Several CourtListener clusters are indexed under a Harvard party-name caption ('Jenkins v. DSHS', 'DSHS v. Luak', 'DSHS v. H.O.', 'R.B. v. C.W.', 'Applebee v. DSHS', 'DSHS v. Gilfillen', 'DSHS v. Hamm', 'Ramsey v. DSHS', 'B.S. v. DSHS', 'DSHS v. T.P.'). case_name here uses the caption the Washington courts use (In re Dependency of K.N.J.; In re Dependency of M.S.R.; In re Parental Rights to B.P.; In re Adoption of T.A.W.; In re Dependency of A.M.; In re Dependency of T.L.G.; In re Dependency of S.M.H.; In re Dependency of V.R.R.; In re Welfare of H.S.; In re Welfare of A.W.), which each cluster's case_name_full confirms. The url therefore contains the CourtListener slug, not the Washington caption.

In re Custody of Smith is reported at 137 Wn.2d 1, 969 P.2d 21 (1998) and was affirmed sub nom. Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000). CourtListener's cluster records date_filed as 2000-03-01 (an amendment/reconsideration entry), so date_decided and year here mirror the CourtListener record while the citation gives the reported 1998 year. Troxel itself was deliberately not quoted because its controlling opinion is a four-Justice plurality rather than a majority.

No published Washington appellate decision was found construing RCW 13.34.267 (extended foster care) or dependency jurisdiction past age 18; targeted searches of both wash and washctapp returned zero results. OUT-04 is therefore served by the authorities that define an older youth's own interests in continued care and representation (Braam, In re Dependency of M.S.R., In re Dependency of E.H.) rather than by an extended-foster-care merits decision. Practitioners should treat OUT-04 as statute-governed.

No published Washington appellate decision was found on children missing from foster care, on CAPTA section 5106a(c) Citizen Review Panels, or on a state child fatality review commission. PMC-03, PMC-04 and PMC-06 are served by the nearest governing Washington authority on systemic oversight (Braam, H.B.H.) and on public access to dependency records (In re Dependency of M.H.P., Wright, In re Dependency of E.H.). PMC-04 carries only two cases because nothing further on point exists.

Washington recognizes an implied statutory tort of negligent investigation under RCW 26.44.050 that has no general common-law analogue. Its boundaries are set by Tyner (parents are within the protected class), M.W. (only harmful placement decisions are actionable), Ducote (stepparents are excluded) and Wrigley (only a report of past or ongoing abuse triggers the duty). Roberson v. Perez, 156 Wn.2d 33 (2005), further rejecting 'constructive placement' claims, is cited within Wrigley but was not separately retrieved and so is not listed.

Reporter immunity under RCW 26.44.060 and custody immunity under RCW 26.44.056(3) are qualified and conditioned on good faith. Dunning v. Paccerelli holds good faith is ordinarily a question of fact and rejects absolute immunity for central-registry listing; Miles shows good faith can nonetheless be resolved as a matter of law where the caseworker relied on treating physicians.

ICWA/WICWA coverage in Washington is broader than the federal floor in three respects confirmed here: the 'reason to know' trigger is met by any participant's indication of tribal heritage (Z.J.G.); the acts protect a non-Indian parent of an Indian child and reach stepparent adoptions (T.A.W.); and the existing Indian family exception is legislatively abrogated (T.A.W.). Caution: In re Dependency of A.M. (2001) predates both WICWA (ch. 13.38 RCW, 2011) and the 2016 BIA regulations; its holding on the standard of proof for 25 U.S.C. 1912(d) should be checked against current 25 C.F.R. part 23 before being relied on.

Chapter 13.50 RCW, not the Public Records Act, is the exclusive route to Washington juvenile dependency records (Wright, following Deer v. DSHS, 122 Wn. App. 84 (2004), which was located but not separately retrieved). A PRA request for such records cannot generate a PRA violation or penalty. Public access to the dependency court file is governed instead by GR 15 and article I, section 10 (In re Dependency of M.H.P.), and confidentiality survives appeal (In re Dependency of E.H.).

Section 1983 authority for FAIL-02 comes from the Ninth Circuit, which governs Washington. Two of the five listed cases, Devereaux v. Abbey (en banc) and Costanich v. DSHS, arise directly out of Washington child welfare investigations. Greene v. Camreta, 588 F.3d 1011 (9th Cir. 2009), the leading in-school child-interview case, was retrieved but is not listed because it was vacated in part as moot (661 F.3d 1201) after Camreta v. Greene, 563 U.S. 692 (2011); Mann v. County of San Diego relies on its reasoning and is listed instead.

The key_cases already present in the WA node files (e.g. 'In re Recall of Olsen', 'In re Disciplinary Proceeding Against Flood') are keyword-matched noise carrying synthetic 'Washington Supreme Court Case <docket>' citations and Justia URLs. Each was checked by title and none is child-welfare authority; none was retained.

Missing (for a later pass): Roberson v. Perez, 156 Wn.2d 33, 123 P.3d 844 (2005) — the brief's own notes admit this was never retrieved. It is one of the four boundary cases for the RCW 26.44.050 implied tort (rejecting 'constructive placement' and limiting who may recover), and DEC-01, DEC-02 and ACT-03 are incomplete without it. Citing Wrigley for a proposition Roberson actually holds is the kind of second-hand sourcing that gets caught.

Missing (for a later pass): Babcock v. State, 116 Wn.2d 596, 809 P.2d 143 (1991) — the controlling Washington Supreme Court authority on absolute versus qualified immunity for DSHS caseworkers in placement and investigation. Dunning and Tyner both build directly on it, yet the brief cites neither the case nor its holding. Belongs at DEC-03, DEC-04 and FAIL-02.

Missing (for a later pass): Yonker v. Department of Social & Health Services, 85 Wn. App. 71, 930 P.2d 958 (1997) — the origin of the implied negligent-investigation cause of action and the source of the case-by-case duty-triggering-report test that Wrigley expressly adopts (Wrigley quotes it at 85 Wn. App. 81). INP-01, INP-02, INP-06 and INP-08 all rest on a rule the brief attributes to Wrigley but that Yonker actually announced.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Welfare of Sego, 82 Wn.2d 736, 513 P.2d 831 (1973) — the foundational Washington case defining 'clear, cogent and convincing' in termination proceedings as requiring the ultimate fact to be shown 'highly probable.' OUT-02 and FAIL-01 recite the standard through K.N.J. and S.M.H. without citing the case that established it.

Missing (for a later pass): Seattle Times Co. v. Ishikawa, 97 Wn.2d 30, 640 P.2d 716 (1982) — M.H.P.'s holding is that the juvenile court failed to perform an Ishikawa analysis, but the brief never cites Ishikawa itself. PMC-05, PMC-06 and FAIL-06 state a sealing standard without supplying the five-factor test that is the standard.

Missing (for a later pass): Lassiter v. Department of Social Services, 452 U.S. 18 (1981) — the federal baseline on appointed counsel in termination proceedings, expressly relied on in M.S.R.'s Mathews analysis. FAIL-01 and OUT-04 discuss counsel rights with no federal anchor.

Missing (for a later pass): Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000) — the brief deliberately omits it because the controlling opinion is a plurality, but In re Custody of Smith was affirmed sub nom. Troxel, and no practitioner will accept ACT-04 or OUT-03 briefed on the state decision alone. Cite it with the plurality caveat rather than omitting it.

Missing (for a later pass): Wallis v. Spencer, 202 F.3d 1126 (9th Cir. 2000) — the Ninth Circuit's foundational authority on warrantless removal AND on medical/forensic examination of seized children without parental notice; Keates and Mann both build on it. INP-12, ACT-06 and FAIL-02 cite the progeny without the root.

Missing (for a later pass): Rogers v. County of San Joaquin, 487 F.3d 1288 (9th Cir. 2007) — the source of the 'imminent danger of serious bodily injury' formulation that Keates quotes and Kirkpatrick applies. Quoting Keates' gloss instead of Rogers' rule weakens INP-12 and DEC-04.

Missing (for a later pass): Deer v. Department of Social & Health Services, 122 Wn. App. 84 (2004) — the brief's notes concede Wright follows Deer and that Deer was located but never retrieved. PMC-05 and FAIL-06 rest on a rule Deer established; relying on Wright's characterization of it is second-hand.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Dependency of Ramquist, 52 Wn. App. 854, 765 P.2d 30 (1988) — the origin of the rule, quoted in A.M., that a parent's unwillingness or inability to use offered services excuses the State from providing more. ACT-02 states this rule through two layers of quotation instead of citing its source.

GAP-CLOSING PASS, 2026-09-21. All eleven authorities the verifier named were located on CourtListener, retrieved and read in this session, and all eleven proved real and on point; none was unverifiable. The 'Missing (for a later pass)' notes above are retained verbatim as the audit trail of what this pass was asked to fix, and are now superseded by the 'Added' notes that follow. No existing case entry was altered.

Added Roberson v. Perez (cluster 4908519) for DEC-01, DEC-02 and ACT-03: the fourth boundary case for the RCW 26.44.050 implied tort, holding the action reaches only an investigation that produces an actual State placement decision and expressly refusing to extend it to 'constructive placement.' Note for accuracy: Roberson assumes without deciding whether the same action lies against law enforcement (the defendant was Douglas County, not DSHS), so it is deliberately NOT mapped to INP-03.

Added Babcock v. State (cluster 1196412) for INP-04, DEC-04 and ACT-03: the controlling Washington authority holding that DSHS caseworkers have no absolute immunity for placement decisions made outside an adversarial judicial process, that they may claim only the Guffey qualified immunity, and that the State itself has no immunity. It is mapped to INP-04 because the majority holds that a court order procured ex parte, without any adversarial evaluation of the placement, confers no immunity on the caseworkers who obtained it. It is not mapped to FAIL-02 because it is a state tort and immunity decision, not a section 1983 removal case.

Added Yonker v. DSHS (cluster 6993314) for INP-01, INP-02, INP-06, INP-08, DEC-01 and DEC-02: the origin of the enforceable chapter 26.44 RCW investigative duty and the express source of the case-by-case duty-triggering-report test that Wrigley later adopts. The quoted sentence is Yonker's own formulation of that test.

Added In re Welfare of Sego (cluster 1306553) for OUT-02 and FAIL-01: the foundational Washington holding that permanent deprivation requires clear, cogent and convincing evidence and that the ultimate fact must be shown to be highly probable, together with the corresponding substantial-evidence-in-light-of-the-highly-probable-test standard of appellate review.

Added Seattle Times Co. v. Ishikawa (cluster 1194165) for FAIL-06, PMC-05 and PMC-06: supplies the five-step closure and sealing analysis whose omission was the actual violation found in In re Dependency of M.H.P. The quote is the majority's announcement of the mandatory steps; the five steps themselves are summarised in the holding because no single sentence of the opinion states all five.

Added Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County (cluster 110506) for OUT-04 and FAIL-01: the federal due process baseline for appointed counsel in termination proceedings, on which In re Dependency of M.S.R.'s Mathews v. Eldridge analysis rests. It is not added to OUT-02, which is already at the six-case ceiling with the authorities that govern the substantive termination standard.

Added Troxel v. Granville (cluster 1087668) for ACT-04 and OUT-03, with the caveat the brief previously used to justify omitting it: the controlling opinion is a four-Justice plurality by Justice O'Connor, and the quoted sentence is from that plurality, not from a majority of the Court. It is included because In re Custody of Smith was affirmed sub nom. Troxel and no practitioner will accept a kinship-placement or guardianship argument briefed on the state decision alone. Brief it as a plurality.

Added Wallis v. Spencer (cluster 7079922) for INP-07, INP-12, ACT-06 and FAIL-02: the Ninth Circuit root of both the warrantless-removal rule and the investigatory-medical-examination rule that Keates and Mann apply. The quoted clause states the notice-and-judicial-approval requirement; the same sentence carries an exception, for a reasonable concern that physical evidence will dissipate or an urgent medical problem requiring immediate attention, which is stated in the holding but could not be quoted intact because the opinion embeds a Schmerber citation inside that clause.

Added Rogers v. County of San Joaquin (cluster 797914) for INP-03, INP-12, DEC-04 and FAIL-02: the source of the 'likely to experience serious bodily harm in the time that would be required to obtain a warrant' formulation that Keates quotes and Kirkpatrick applies, and the case in which the Ninth Circuit denied a social worker qualified immunity outright for a non-exigent removal.

Added Deer v. Department of Social & Health Services (cluster 4937668) for FAIL-06, PMC-05 and PMC-06: the decision Wright follows, holding that chapter 13.50 RCW is an 'other statute' exemption that supplements the Public Records Act and supplies the exclusive process, a motion in juvenile court, for obtaining juvenile justice and care records.

Added In re Dependency of Ramquist (cluster 1170805) for ACT-01 and ACT-02: the origin of the rule, quoted in In re Dependency of A.M., that a parent's unwillingness or inability to use the services provided excuses the State from offering more. CourtListener indexes this cluster under the Harvard party caption 'New Hope of Washington v. Ramquist'; the cluster's case_name_full ('In the Matter of the Dependency of Zachary Ramquist') confirms the Washington caption used here, so the url carries the CourtListener slug rather than the Washington caption. It is not added to OUT-02, which is at the six-case ceiling.

Added Petcu v. State (cluster 4937237) for INP-04 and DEC-05, beyond the eleven authorities the verifier named. INP-04 (court-ordered referral) previously had no mapped case at all, even though Tyner's own relevance object claimed it. Petcu, a Wenatchee-derived negligent-investigation case, states the operative Tyner rule for that node: a dependency court order is a superseding intervening cause cutting off caseworker liability unless the faulty investigation deprived the court of material information.

node_map reconciliation: the reconciled brief's node_map omitted many nodes that the existing case entries' own relevance objects already claimed. INP-04, INP-05 and PMC-02 were empty although Tyner declared INP-04, A.L.K. and H.Q. declared INP-05, and Braam, Costanich and Hardee declared PMC-02; Tyner was absent from INP-01, DEC-02 and ACT-05; Miles and Keates were absent from INP-03; M.W. and Mann were absent from INP-07; H.B.H. and M.H.P. were absent from INP-09; B.P. and C.S. were absent from ACT-01; Wrigley was absent from ACT-04; E.H. and M.S.R. were absent from OUT-04; D.S. was absent from OUT-05; M.S.R. was absent from FAIL-03 and PMC-01; E.H. was absent from PMC-03. Every existing case is now mapped to each node its own relevance object names.

Ceiling rebalancing: to keep every node within the 2-6 case limit after these additions, four existing mappings were moved rather than duplicated. Hardee v. DSHS and In re Dependency of S.M.H. were dropped from FAIL-01 (already at six) to make room for Sego and Lassiter, the foundational authorities for that node; both remain in the brief and remain mapped elsewhere (Hardee at DEC-03 and PMC-02, S.M.H. at ACT-05). Miles v. CPS and Mann v. County of San Diego were dropped from FAIL-02 in favour of Wallis and Rogers; Miles remains at INP-03, INP-07, INP-12 and DEC-04, and Mann remains at INP-07, INP-12 and ACT-06.

Date fields mirror the CourtListener cluster record, and two of them differ from the reported decision date. CourtListener records Lassiter's date_filed as 1981-08-28 although the opinion is reported as decided June 1, 1981. CourtListener records Wallis's date_filed as 1999-09-14, which is the date of the superseded opinion at 193 F.3d 1054; the citation given here, 202 F.3d 1126, is the amended opinion filed on rehearing in 2000, which is the text that was read and quoted. Confirm both dates against the official reporter before filing.

Coverage after this pass: all 42 nodes carry between 2 and 6 cases. PMC-04 (fatality review commission) remains at two, Braam and H.B.H., because no Washington decision on a state child fatality review commission or on CAPTA citizen review panels exists; targeted searches again returned nothing on point. The brief now carries 45 distinct cases, above the 20-40 target, because this reconciliation pass added twelve foundational authorities without removing any existing entry.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Dependency of Schermer, 161 Wn.2d 927, 169 P.3d 452 (2007) — the brief's own notes name Schermer and supply its parallel cite as if it were in the brief, but there is NO case entry for it. It is leading Washington Supreme Court authority on the dependency standard and the constitutional limits on State intervention short of termination, and its absence is a self-inflicted internal inconsistency a reviewing lawyer will catch immediately. Belongs at DEC-05 and OUT-03.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Dependency of K.N.J., 171 Wn.2d 568, 257 P.3d 522 (2011) — same defect: the brief's caption-reconciliation note lists 'In re Dependency of K.N.J.' as the Washington caption for a cluster, and a later note says 'OUT-02 and FAIL-01 recite the standard through K.N.J. and S.M.H.,' yet no K.N.J. entry exists anywhere in the case list. It holds a termination order entered without a properly issued summons is void, which is genuine authority for FAIL-01 and would fill the hole OUT-05 is left with after dropping In re Guardianship of D.S.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Custody of Smith, 137 Wn.2d 1, 969 P.2d 21 (1998) — the brief devotes an entire note to explaining how it handles Smith's date and its affirmance sub nom. Troxel, but Smith itself is not in the case list. It is the Washington Supreme Court decision striking the nonparental visitation statutes and remains the controlling state-law statement of the fit-parent presumption, which matters because Troxel's controlling opinion is only a plurality. ACT-04 and OUT-03 currently rest on a plurality with no state-law anchor.

Missing (for a later pass): Guffey v. State, 103 Wn.2d 144, 690 P.2d 1163 (1984) — the source of the qualified-immunity standard that Babcock applies by name ('the trial court did not apply the Guffey standard to these caseworkers'; 'Lack of malice is necessary but not sufficient to establish qualified immunity under Guffey'). I confirmed these references in the Babcock majority text retrieved this session. The brief now states the Guffey three-element test through Babcock's restatement of it without ever citing Guffey — exactly the second-hand sourcing the brief's own earlier notes condemned. Belongs at DEC-03, DEC-04 and ACT-03.

Missing (for a later pass): Coverdell v. Department of Social & Health Services, 834 F.2d 758 (9th Cir. 1987) — confirmed in the Babcock majority text, which distinguishes it at length: a caseworker who removes a child BECAUSE a court specifically ordered the removal receives absolute immunity. That is the single most directly on-point authority for INP-04 (court-ordered referral), a node the brief concedes had no mapped case at all before Petcu was added, and it supplies the rule's positive side where Babcock supplies only the negative.

Missing (for a later pass): Lesley v. Department of Social & Health Services, 83 Wn.
